title: Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture
formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every finite nonempty tree \(T\) and every integer \(r\ge1\), there exists an integer \(B\ge0\) such that every finite simple undirected graph \(G\) satisfies
\[\bigl(\omega(G)\le r\ \land\ G\text{ has no induced copy of }T\bigr)
\ \Longrightarrow\ \chi(G)\le B.\]
The quantifier order is \(\forall T\,\forall r\,\exists B\,\forall G\). The bound may depend on the entire tree \(T\) and on \(r\), but must be independent of the number of vertices and every other parameter of \(G\). No rate of growth or computational requirement on \(B\) is prescribed.
definitions:
Graphs and trees. A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) consists of a finite vertex set and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops or multiple edges. A path has distinct vertices, with adjacent consecutive vertices; a cycle has at least three distinct vertices with consecutive and last-to-first adjacency. A tree is a nonempty connected graph containing no cycle. Connected means that each pair of vertices is joined by a path. The one-vertex tree is allowed. Host graphs need not be connected and may have no vertices. Equivalently, one may quantify over graphs with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) for every integer \(n\ge0\), with \([0]=\varnothing\); labels have no mathematical significance.

Induced exclusion. For \(S\subseteq V(G)\), the graph \(G[S]\) has vertex set \(S\) and exactly the edges of \(G\) with both ends in \(S\). An induced copy of \(T\) is an injective map \(\varphi:V(T)\to V(G)\) such that for all distinct \(u,v\in V(T)\),
\[\{u,v\}\in E(T)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\{\varphi(u),\varphi(v)\}\in E(G).\]
A graph is \(T\)-free when no such map exists. The requirement preserves nonedges as well as edges. It is different from excluding an ordinary subgraph, a minor or a subdivision of \(T\). Edges from the image to vertices outside it are unrestricted.

Clique and chromatic numbers. A clique is a vertex subset whose distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent. Its maximum possible size is \(\omega(G)\). A proper \(k\)-colouring is a map \(c:V(G)\to[k]\) with \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). The least nonnegative integer \(k\) admitting such a map is \(\chi(G)\). Thus both parameters are zero for the empty graph, and every nonempty edgeless graph has both equal to one. The bound \(\omega(G)\le r\) is equivalent to excluding a clique on \(r+1\) vertices. Colour classes are independent sets, meaning subsets with no adjacent pair. Colouring here is ordinary vertex colouring, without lists, weights, fractional assignments or edge orientations.

Scope of the bound. Both the tree and the clique bound are fixed before the host graph varies. There is no maximum-degree, girth, geometric-representation, size or other promise on the host. The integer \(B=B(T,r)\) may grow arbitrarily quickly with its two allowed parameters. The target asks for existence of a finite bound, not its minimum value, a polynomial in \(r\), a computable function, or a procedure finding a colouring. There is consequently no input encoding, algorithmic running time or random-error parameter in the proposition.

Equivalent terminology. A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs. The \(T\)-free graphs form such a class. Saying it is \(\chi\)-bounded means that there is a function \(f_T:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that \(\chi(G)\le f_T(\omega(G))\) for every graph in the class. The conjecture asserts this for every nonempty tree; there is no requirement that the same function work for all trees. A negative answer means there are one fixed tree \(T\) and one fixed integer \(r\ge1\) for which chromatic numbers of the permitted hosts have no finite upper bound.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its negation. A positive answer must establish a finite \(B(T,r)\) for every permitted pair and prove the bound for every finite host graph. A nonconstructive existence proof is sufficient; neither a sharp formula nor an efficient colouring algorithm is required.

A negative answer must specify a single finite tree \(T\) and a single integer \(r\ge1\) and prove
\[\forall k\ge1\ \exists G:\quad G\text{ is finite and }T\text{-free},\qquad
\omega(G)\le r,\qquad\chi(G)\ge k.\]
Equivalently, supply such a family \((G_k)_{k\ge1}\) with verified unbounded chromatic number. Changing the excluded tree or clique bound as \(k\) grows does not refute the proposition. One finite example can invalidate a proposed numerical bound but cannot rule out a larger bound.

Bounds depending on host size, special tree families, additional host promises, path-induced copies, or a different colouring parameter do not resolve the full statement. Nor does disproving only a polynomial or computable strengthening refute the unrestricted finite-bound target.
why: Would characterize induced forests as the single forbidden patterns capable of bounding ordinary chromatic number in terms of clique number, clarifying a central structural obstruction to graph colouring and large independent sets.

importance.reason: A central organizing conjecture for hereditary graph colouring and forbidden induced subgraphs, defining the proposed forest boundary for χ-boundedness.

progress.text: Kierstead–Penrice establish \(\chi\)-boundedness when the excluded tree has radius at most two.
Scott–Seymour strengthen radius-two results under complete multipartite subgraph exclusions; checked preprint revised 10 January 2023.
Nguyen–Scott–Seymour force path-induced rooted copies of arbitrary trees, while permitting extra edges between branches.
Nguyen–Scott–Seymour prove near-linear independent sets and subpolynomial chromatic bounds for every fixed forest and clique bound; journal publication 25 September 2025.
Davies–Yuditsky’s journal publication proves polynomial \(\chi\)-boundedness under the additional promise of boxicity bounded by a fixed dimension.

status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected 2025 and April 2026 primary sources still state the general conjecture as open. Their subpolynomial, fractional or fixed-dimension results have weaker conclusions or additional hypotheses. Recent tournament and domatic analogues concern different parameters. No matching full resolution was found in the bounded later-work check; cited proofs were not independently formalized.

context_blocks.text: A large clique forces many colours, but it is not the only obstruction: triangle-free graphs can also require arbitrarily many colours. The conjecture says that each fixed induced tree must eventually appear in every sufficiently high-chromatic graph with a fixed clique bound. Its force lies in independence from graph size; adding vertices cannot keep increasing the required palette while avoiding the same tree.

Ordinary and induced copies encode different restrictions. A triangle contains a three-vertex path as an ordinary subgraph, but does not induce that path because its endpoints are adjacent. More generally, a complete graph contains every tree on at most its number of vertices as an ordinary subgraph, but no induced tree on three or more vertices. The clique restriction alone does not solve the issue: the conjecture must hold for every fixed clique bound, including triangle-free hosts.

The forest boundary has a precise reason. Graphs can have arbitrarily high chromatic number and girth, where girth is the length of a shortest cycle. If an excluded graph contains a cycle, sufficiently large girth avoids that graph while still allowing unbounded chromatic number and no triangles. The nonempty-forest version of the conjecture is equivalent to the all-trees version: every finite forest is an induced subgraph of some finite tree.

Important tree families are known. Kierstead and Penrice proved the radius-at-most-two case in 1994; radius at most two means that some vertex has distance at most two from every other vertex. Scott and Seymour’s later Theorem 1.6 controls chromatic number polynomially in the part size of an excluded complete multipartite ordinary subgraph, for a fixed number of parts and a fixed radius-two tree. Its polynomial statement in that parameter is not a proof of polynomial dependence on clique number for every tree.

The inherited Nguyen–Scott–Seymour paper proves a weaker embedding theorem for every rooted tree: sufficiently high chromatic number at fixed clique bound forces a path-induced copy. Each root-to-vertex path has no extra edge among its own vertices. Edges between separate branches remain possible, so the entire image need not be an induced tree. Its main theorem therefore does not prove the conjecture stated here.

Their near-linear-stable-set theorem applies to every fixed forest and clique bound: an \(n\)-vertex permitted graph has an independent set of size \(n^{1-o(1)}\) and chromatic number \(n^{o(1)}\). In particular, for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), the chromatic bound is eventually at most \(n^\varepsilon\). This is much smaller than any fixed positive power, but can still diverge; \(\log n\) illustrates that distinction.

The same paper bounds fractional chromatic number for multibrooms, obtained by identifying the roots of paths with extra leaves at their far ends. Fractional colouring permits weighted independent sets covering every vertex to total weight at least one; ordinary colouring requires an actual partition. General multibrooms remain an open case of the latter statement in that source.

Davies and Yuditsky’s April 2026 journal theorem treats intersection graphs of axis-aligned boxes in \(\mathbb R^d\), for each fixed dimension \(d\). Vertices represent boxes and adjacency means nonempty intersection. Excluding a fixed induced forest then gives a polynomial bound in clique number, but the polynomial may depend on both the forest and \(d\). This extra dimension parameter prevents the theorem from giving the unrestricted bound in the card.

The conjecture concerns existence of colourings and has consequences for independent-set size, because one colour class must contain at least the number of vertices divided by the number of colours. It does not automatically provide an efficient algorithm for finding either object. Separating the structural assertion from its possible computational refinements keeps the benchmark focused on the established conjecture.
A September 2026 paper studies a tournament analogue using directed clique and chromatic parameters. These differ from the ordinary undirected parameters in this card.
A June 2026 paper instead studies domatic number, which partitions vertices into dominating sets. The shared conjecture name does not make that parameter ordinary chromatic number.

sentences: The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture asks whether excluding any fixed induced tree makes chromatic number bounded at each fixed clique bound.
The host is an arbitrary finite simple undirected graph, and the bound may depend on the tree and clique bound but not on host size.
An accepted answer requires a complete Lean proof, or one fixed tree and clique bound supporting graphs of unbounded chromatic number.
Path-induced copies, fractional colouring and subpolynomial size-dependent bounds are distinct from the selected ordinary-colouring statement.
The conjecture would identify forests as the precise single forbidden-pattern boundary for this form of hereditary graph colouring.
